claims.text: Two-phase coexistence simulations can accurately predict the melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The method can predict melting temperature.
The method can predict entropy of fusion.
The method can predict enthalpy of fusion.
The method can predict the volume change at melting.
A semi-empirical potential or suitably trained machine-learning potential calibrated to DFT data can be used to execute the two-phase coexistence simulations.
Two-phase coexistence simulations using a calibrated potential require only a fraction of the computational cost of full ab initio free-energy methods.
A simulation cell containing preformed solid and liquid regions can be equilibrated near the melting point under periodic boundary conditions.
The solid-liquid interface forms and evolves during a two-phase coexistence simulation.
The solid-liquid interface mediates determination of thermodynamic quantities as the system reaches coexistence.
Equilibration of the solid and liquid phases determines the stable coexistence temperature.
Interface behavior at coexistence enables derivation of latent heat, entropy change, and volume change.
The predicted melting properties will agree closely with results from full ab initio free-energy thermodynamic integration.
Ab initio free-energy thermodynamic integration is an accurate but computationally intensive baseline.
The accuracy of the approach depends on the accuracy of the selected interatomic potential or machine-learning surrogate.
The potential may require recalibration for different classes of refractory materials.
